In the Utah War call-up of 1857 he and Parson served as privates in the same platoon of a Weber District militia company mustered at Ogden, he from October 20 and Parson from November 9 (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, Utah State Archives), and in July 1860 they were next-door neighbors near Ogden, both tanners (1860 U.S. census, Weber County, p. 155). The Morrisites' bugler: he kept sounding the bugle under fire as the fort surrendered on June 15, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137). He moved from Utah to Omaha in 1864 and to Wisner, Nebraska, in 1867, and joined the RLDS Church in 1870 (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2); a descendant's family tradition of a Farley who moved to Nebraska and joined the RLDS Church fits him (see note 9). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Robert Farley”).

name: Bar, Labrach
text: Johann Lebrecht Bar, known as John L. Bear. His account of Morris's death, from "The Autobiography of John L. Bear" (Journal of History, Lamoni, 1911–12), is quoted by Anderson (pp. 138–39). Anderson says he “lost his wife and child in the battle” (p. 138). The Anderson gravestone plaque says that “Mrs. J. L. Bear and her baby were killed with another cannon ball,” after the first shot of June 13, 1862, and Family Tree and a family account give the same date. Anderson, however, says that two women were killed while holding an infant and that in neither case was the child hurt (p. 169 n. 6), so whether the baby died is not settled. He married Barbara Diethelm at Soda Springs on October 12, 1863 (FamilySearch), joined the RLDS Church, and died at Independence in 1919.

name: Eardley, John R.
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). The movement's historian: compiled Gems of Inspiration (1899); a leader of the Montana church. Henry Hendrickson, who grew up among the Montana Morrisites, recalled in 1962 that Eardley, an Englishman, had gone with the group to California and later came back to Montana (interview by Don Cornelius, April 19, 1962, pp. 4–5, OH 018-001, University of Montana). In February 1880, writing from Sacramento to George Thompson, he planned to sell his homestead at Hollister and open “a general merchandise & trading store” in Montana within reach of the church’s members (Church History Library, MS 31876). In January 1882 John R. Eardley, formerly of San Francisco, built the store at Willow Glen and became its postmaster; the legislature confirmed him as a notary public in 1883, and he advertised as a notary, conveyancer and United States land agent at Willow Glen. In January 1889 the territorial Council chose him as its chief clerk, as Hendrickson remembered ( New North-West , January 20 and March 10, 1882; March 2, 1883, p. 2; January 30, 1885, p. 1; January 18, 1889, p. 2). In 1891 he was again a clerk of the legislature at Helena, having left Willow Glen when his rented houses in Anaconda stood empty (Eardley to Hendrickson, February–June 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1891). He was a clerk of the legislature again in the 1893 session and journal clerk of th

name: Dow, Alexander Sr.
text: Eyewitness; his sworn affidavit of April 18, 1863, on Burton's shooting of Morris was widely published (Anderson, pp. 133, 139, 148–49). Spokesman of the Soda Springs company in 1863 (Anderson, p. 159) and an early follower of Cainan (Anderson, p. 168). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, p. 142. His own short account, undated, says he reached Salt Lake City on November 20, 1856, and worked there as a tinsmith before joining Morris, and that he was close to Burton when Burton shot down Morris, Banks, Mrs. Bowman and a Danish woman. By 1870 he was in St. Louis, where a dispute with the Reorganized Church branch led Joseph Smith III to advise him to ask its forgiveness (Plano, August 1870). In March 1873 he wrote to Smith from 1323 North Eighth Street, protesting that the church had refused to receive him and saying he still held the faith he had embraced at his baptism in 1843. His papers, with manuscripts of Morris’s revelations, are the Joseph Morris Papers (P11-1 f4–f5, Community of Christ Library Archives). In August 1874 S. P. Guhl reported that Morris’s apostles had organized in California, with John Parson as president and R. J. Livingston and Dow as his counselors (S. P. Guhl to Andrew Hendrickson, Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Probably the “Dow” whom Williams in 1868 named, with Davies and “Gudmanson,” among the ministers he had sent

name: Firth, John
text: One of the six founding members of the church, April 6, 1861 (Anderson, p. 66); ordained a high priest (Spirit Prevails, p. 77; Anderson, p. 65). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 51–52. Family Tree (FamilySearch KWVG-KDB, born 1823) places him at South Weber; his sons William H. and Arthur are also on the roll. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Firth”). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 33 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 9024). Price’s journal names him among the same six (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Kendell, William
text: One of the six founding members, April 6, 1861 (Anderson, p. 66, as Kendall); among the first apostles (Anderson, p. 67); ordained a high priest (Spirit Prevails, p. 77). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, p. 45. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “William Kendall”). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (seven files, 60 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 16620). Price’s journal names him among the same six (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Jones, John E.
text: Ordained an apostle in June 1861 (Anderson, p. 67; Spirit Prevails, p. 102). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name him among the seven sentenced in March 1863 and pardoned (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31), but the court report says the jury found him not guilty of murder; he then pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Later with James Dove and John Livingstone in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 143, 177, 180). He “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library).

name: Klemgard, Peter C.
text: Led the armed party of about thirty that captured William Jones and his companions (Anderson, p. 99, as Klemgaard); named in the writs and the contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); appointed to take charge of the firearms (Spirit Prevails, pp. 527–29). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree for the deaths of the posse men and sentenced to fifteen years at hard labor, the heaviest sentence (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); Governor Harding pardoned him a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31). He later followed William W. Davies. Testifying at Walla Walla in 1881, he said that he and Davies had withdrawn from the Latter-day Saint church under Morris at Weber, that he next met Davies at Soda Springs in 1865, where there were “about sixty of us Morrisites” and the camp broke up for want of a leader, and that he then went to San Francisco, where Davies’s missionaries won him over. He lived at Davies’s camp near Walla Walla with his wife and four children from April 1870 to April 1872, and added that “the doctrine taught at the Davies camp is not like the Morrisite religion” (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Taylor, Abraham
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). A revelation explains the death of his child (Spirit Prevails, p. 115). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor (Deseret News, April 1, 1863), and pardoned a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31); forfeited bail, and his homestead was sold (Anderson, p. 148). He bought the chest of Morris's revelations, which Hannah Banks had buried in the Bowery, and kept it for over twenty years; it passed to his son Joseph (Spirit Prevails, "Concerning the Revelations"). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (four files, 14 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 31954). An Abraham Taylor testified at Burton’s trial in March 1879 that he had been in the fort at the surrender; he gave his home as Salt Lake City’s Twelfth Ward ( Salt Lake Herald , Mar. 4, 1879). The 1870 and 1880 censuses place this Abraham Taylor at Springville, so either he was living in Salt Lake City for a time or the witness was another man.

name: Gudmundson, Gudmund
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). An artist: Morris directed him to draw the white horse larger than in his drawing of the twelve generals, and to make the crowns for the Foreshadowing (Spirit Prevails, pp. 532, 583). Later prominent among the scattered congregations (Anderson, p. 157). Almost certainly the “Gudmanson” whom Williams in 1868 named with Dow and Davies among the “rebels”: George Thompson wrote in 1869 of “Poor Goodman Goodmunsen, poor W. W. Davis and others of the Weber House, good men,” who had been “deceived by supernatural manifestations” (George Thompson to William P. Thomas, July 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874).

name: Jacobson, Niels
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67, as Neils Jacobsen). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, p. 257 and No. 211, Weber, January 28, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, pp. 391–94). Forscutt’s diary has “Niels Jacobsen Geertzen,” “an Apostle of the new faith,” leaving the camp with a man named Jensen on January 23, 1862; he came back after five days, confessed, gave up his apostleship and was received into the quorum of priests (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). The revelation of January 28 falls within those days.

name: Trolsen, John
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67). Revelation concerning him, Jacobsen and Niels Morrisen: Spirit Prevails, p. 257. Probably John Trolson (1820–1898; FamilySearch LCRZ-RQ8), father of Anton Trolson, who is also on the roll; the family settled in Nevada. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, where “John Trolsom” is probably this man).

name: Harris, William
text: Called by revelation to preside over the priests of Aaron (Spirit Prevails, p. 102); directed to wear a robe and carry a rod foreshadowing Aaron's on Foreshadowing Day (Spirit Prevails, pp. 551–59). The pencil list of officers marks him Bishop. Josiah D. Price copied the declaration Harris made in the bishop’s robe on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, 1862 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). In April 1873 Forscutt, on a Reorganized Church mission in South Wales, met a Mrs. Eastman, “the sister of William Harris, formerly Bishop of the Morrisite Church,” whom Latter-day Saint missionaries had told that her brother was “an associate of thieves and robbers” (Forscutt, journal, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University, April 30, 1873).

name: Guhl, Soren Peter
text: Soren Peter Guhl (1821–1883), born in Jutland, Denmark, who came to Utah in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJ8-9RQ). Held to bail after the siege as “S. P. Guhl” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Leader of the Council Bluffs group; sustained as Cainan’s first counselor on January 24, 1869, having come to Omaha on January 22 “from Montana, where he had lived some years”; he organized the Council Bluffs and Omaha congregations on February 7, 1869, and presided over them until May 30, 1869 (Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876); and sent on a mission to Denmark, where he broke with Cainan (Anderson, pp. 193–94); in October 1869 Williams wrote that “the important request from Denmark for money is altogether against my wishes,” and that Guhl “likes to take some other way,” to which Williams consented only because of “his often importunities” (Williams to the Omaha church, October 13, 1869, MS 31876); Cainan had written ahead to Deer Lodge to receive him on his way to Scandinavia (Anderson, p. 187), and later named him among the “traitors” (Anderson, p. 204). He died at Council Bluffs, Iowa, in 1883. In a letter of November 24, 1874, from 678 14th Street, Omaha, to William James and the Saints in Montana, Guhl wrote that Cainan had ordered him and “Bro. Poulsen” to organize the church at Omaha and had told him, in a letter of October 3, 1874, that his mission stood “under his especial direction” and not under Deer Lodge. He r

name: Magee, William
text: Named as bearer of the second rod for the Foreshadowing; its inscription begins "Behold, I am William Magee, even number two" (Spirit Prevails, p. 559). Probably William Magee (1826–1890; FamilySearch KWJD-PC3), who died at Wadsworth, Nevada; his daughter Ellen is also on the roll.

name: Park, Hugh
text: His name was inscribed on the fifth scepter: "Hugh Park … even number five" (Anderson, p. 117). The Woodruff Papers identify him as the Hugh Park named on a scepter recovered after the surrender (FamilySearch note). Son of David and Ann Brooks Park (FamilySearch LLQF-CF6, KWJ5-6FF), who settled at Mottsville in the Carson Valley, Nevada; his parents and his siblings David Jr., Martha, Ellen and Joseph Hyrum are probably the roll's other Park entries. The inscription on his rod, copied from the original on June 19, 1862, reads: “Behold! I am Hugh Park—even number five,” standing “in the stead of the fifth first born son of Adam” (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). Taken at the surrender, aged 18, born in Canada (same list).

name: Banks, John
text: Joseph Morris's counselor in the church presidency and, in Forscutt's words, the movement's orator; a member of the First Council (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 24, 51); signed letters with Morris and Richard Cook (Spirit Prevails). Named with Morris, Cook, Parson and Klemgard in the May 1862 writ over the three imprisoned dissenters (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20). Wounded at the surrender on June 15, 1862, and died that evening in custody (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Anderson, p. 137); Eardley reports he seemed to be recovering in a wagon, then was dead within the hour, citing William Jones, who went to the wagon (Gems, p. 28). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 1668). On May 1, 1862, he rode the black horse carrying a pair of balances, and on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, he rode as the third general (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives). His son Franklin Cyrus Banks (1847–1922) settled at Pleasant Grove; two of Franklin’s sons wrote about him: John Ray Banks (1881–1940), in his University of Utah thesis of 1909, “A Document History of the Morrisites in Utah,” and Karl Banks (b. 1889), in an essay and in talks of 1958–72 (see the Bibliography, Repositories and Newspapers; family links from FamilySearch Family Tree, KWJC-LR7, KWVR-2WN).

name: Cook, Richard
text: Bishop of the LDS South Weber Ward when Morris arrived, and the first to hear his claims there (Anderson, pp. 52, 62); then in Morris's presidency. Named in the May 1862 writ and contempt citation (Anderson, pp. 101–8; Gems, p. 20); called out by Burton at the surrender (Gems, p. 28). After the war a leader with John Parson in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178, 180). Summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 28). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 37, 39, 93, 364–67, 459–61; appointment, Spirit Prevails, p. 77. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Richard Cook”). At the March 1863 term the prosecution dropped the murder charge against him (nolle prosequi); he pleaded guilty to resisting an officer and was fined $100, and the $50 fine for contempt of June 1862 was remitted (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Josiah D. Price names him first of the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, to found his church, all made high priests (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives); a revelation of April 4 names him and John Parson as the first two called (Spirit Prevails, No. 56, pp. 78–79). On May 1, 1862, he rode the red horse with a sword before the companies, and on Foreshadowing Day, May 30, he rode as the sec

name: Cook, John
text: Richard Cook's brother. Met Morris near the Warm Springs and brought him to South Weber, the turning point in Morris's career (Anderson, pp. 51–52, 62; Gems, pp. 12, 16). One of the six founding members of the church, April 6, 1861 (Anderson, p. 66); ordained a high priest (Spirit Prevails, p. 77) and among the first apostles (Anderson, p. 67). Revelations concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 38, 459–61. A member of the First Council; summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28, 51). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “John Cook”). Price’s journal also names him among the six baptized on April 6, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Parson, John
text: Living up Weber Canyon when Morris began his mission (Gems, p. 16); called by revelation to move to South Weber, February 1861, with Robert Farley (Spirit Prevails, pp. 60–61); president of the apostles (Anderson, p. 65; Spirit Prevails, p. 77). Gave the order to raise the white flag at the surrender (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137); named in the writ and contempt citation (Anderson, p. 108; Gems, p. 20). Carried Governor Harding's pardon to the penitentiary and demanded the seven prisoners' release (Gems, p. 31). Later a leader in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178–81). A member of the First Council; summoned before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 28, 51). In November 1857 he served as a private in the same Weber District militia company and platoon as Robert Farley, mustered at Ogden in the Utah War call-up (Utah Territorial Militia Records, series 2210, Utah State Archives); in July 1860 the two were next-door neighbors near Ogden, both tanners (1860 U.S. census, Weber County, p. 155, as "Jno Parsons"). He later joined the RLDS Church: Joseph Smith III baptized him at Oakland, California, over the protests of some of his brethren, and on July 29, 1889, Parson showed Smith and Brother Anthony the site of the camp at Weber (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, pp. 432–33). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodru

name: Forscutt, Mark Hill
text: Ordained an apostle in June 1861 (Anderson, p. 67); named in revelations with John E. Jones (Spirit Prevails, p. 100) and John Parson (Spirit Prevails, p. 128), and in Morris's notice to Parson and Forscutt to close the office, August 30, 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 675); a member of the First Council, and fined $56.80 by the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 34, 51); later an RLDS minister. Joseph Smith III, who counted him an early friend, preached his funeral at Nebraska City in October 1903 (Joseph Smith III and the Restoration, 1952, p. 433). His "Sketch of Joseph Morris" (Church History Library, MS 702) is the subject of the editor's documentary edition, in preparation. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (44 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 36981). He was one of eight men who “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library).

name: Dove, James
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67); led the Nevada and California Morrisites (Anderson, ch. 13, pp. 177–87). His writings are in Watson. Fined $56.80 by the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 34).

name: Brown, Alonzo
text: Lived with his wife in the Kington schoolhouse, where rowdies attacked them in November 1861; named in the complaint that followed (Anderson, p. 82). Carried the white flag at the surrender on June 15, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 7; Anderson, p. 137). Fined $56.80 by the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training; Forscutt also tells the schoolhouse incident (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 34, 38). A Morrisite account of 1891 says that John Parson took him to carry the flag when he went out to surrender to Judson Stoddard (“Massacre of Morrisites,” letter 9 of “The Elder,” Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891, p. 3).

name: Anderson, Niels
text: At the fort during the siege; later said the posse allowed too little time to surrender (Anderson, p. 114). Married Mary Christofferson (probably Christofferson, Maria), wounded by the first cannon shot of the siege, on July 30, 1863, and was among the few Morrisites who stayed at Soda Springs (Anderson, p. 162); Shupe gives the date as July 20, 1863, calls theirs the first marriage in Idaho Territory, and says he was the blacksmith at Connor's post (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Their son Abraham C. Anderson was born on February 20, 1865 (Shupe, p. 16). The family's gravestone plaque at Soda Springs calls him “the father of the Anti-Mormon Party” in Idaho, and a National Park Service marker there says he and other Morrisites began the anti-polygamy campaign that ended in the Idaho test oath barring Mormons from voting. He bought 160 acres near Soda Springs as a cash entry at the Oxford land office, patented January 20, 1882 (Boise Meridian, T9S R41E, sec. 3; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-ID0010__.029). The 1880 U.S. census finds him at Soda Springs, “Nels Anderson”, born in Denmark about 1835 (1880 U.S. census). He died in 1926 (FamilySearch LC37-Q71). His 1903 letter to Joseph F. Smith is cited in Anderson's bibliography (Anderson, p. 237). At Burton’s trial in February 1879, after his wife had testified for the prosecution, the defense offered to prove that he had written to Burton offering, for payment, to keep her out of the way, as compensat

name: Eliason, Erick
text: Erik Eliasson (1817–1893), born in Västmanland, Sweden (FamilySearch MVRH-QQ6). Shupe names Eric Eliason among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He and his wife Karin (Eliason, Karen) stayed with the Morrisites at Soda Springs, where four of their six children were born between 1863 and 1869; their daughter Anna, born August 2, 1863, is the Anna Eliason whom Shupe calls the first white child born at Soda Springs (p. 29). Baptized into the RLDS Church at Soda Springs on June 9, 1870, by Lars Edler (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2). A grandson's account says Erik left part of the family at Soda Springs and drove to the Deer Lodge Valley with his ten-year-old twins, Jacob and John, and settled on the ranch near Racetrack that the family still held in 1989 (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109). The account dates the move to 1868, but the twins were born in 1867 and a son was born at Soda Springs in 1869, so the move came later than 1868. The 1880 U.S. census counts Erik three times: as a married farmer living alone in the Deer Lodge Valley, Montana (ED 11, p. 154d); as a rancher living alone at Soda Springs (ED 25, p. 287b); and, as “Alexr. Eliasson”, 63, at the head of the family at Soda Springs, with “Carrie”, 50, and all six children, the thirteen-year-old twins among them (ED 25, p. 289a). In June 1880, then, he was already farming in Montana while the family’s h

name: Eliason, Karen
text: Karin Caroline Anderson (1830–1902), wife of Erik Eliasson (FamilySearch LHN8-4C5). Shupe lists Mrs. Caroline Eliason among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Baptized into the RLDS Church with her husband on June 9, 1870, as Caroline Eliasson (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2). They had four sons and two daughters: Caroline (born 1861 at Farmington, Utah), Anna, Joseph, the twins Jacob and John, and Isaac, the last five born at Soda Springs. When Erik took the twins to the Deer Lodge Valley, part of the family stayed at Soda Springs (Powell County: Where It All Began, pp. 108–109); Karin died there in 1902. In June 1880 “Carrie Eliasson”, 50, was at Soda Springs with all six children (1880 U.S. census, Oneida County, Idaho, ED 25, p. 289a), while Erik was also counted farming in the Deer Lodge Valley. Identified by her descendant Keith Chappelow. Probably the Caroline Eliason who testified at Burton’s trial in February 1879 that she had belonged to the Morrisites at Weber in 1862 and remembered the armed men arriving on the Friday morning ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 21, 1879).

name: Smith, Hans Peter
text: Called to the apostleship (Spirit Prevails, p. 412). Hans Peter Smith (1811–1868; FamilySearch KJP1-Y7Z): Family Tree records his call at Kington Fort in February 1862 as one of the Morrisite Twelve Apostles, and a later residence at Carson City, Nevada.

name: Anderson, Abelone
text: Probably Appelone Maria Andersdatter (1816–1884), wife of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch KWVH-NZM); Andersdatter is the Danish form of Anderson, so she would be listed under her own patronymic. Mother of Mary Christoffersen Anderson. She died at Soda Springs in 1884.

name: Beck, Niels R.
text: Niels Rasmussen Beck (1823–1888; FamilySearch KWJ4-LNP). Family Tree describes him as a Morrisite and records his death at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1888. His is the earliest Morrisite land patent found in the Deer Lodge Valley: a 160-acre preemption cash entry at the Helena land office, patented May 1, 1871 (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, secs. 34–35; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0070__.167). A preemption claimant had to prove when he settled on the land, so the case file at the National Archives should date his arrival. A “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” sent gifts by letter and money order to William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla, the first of them toward the purchase of its eighty acres, according to Swen O. Hagg’s testimony in 1881, and a list of donations filed in the same case credits “Neils R. Beck” with $4,839 between 1866 and 1878. Davies himself testified that he had received “over $1500 from Mr. Beck to pay for land,” $300 for a printing press and more than $3,000 besides, all sent in his name “for the house of the Lord,” and that “Mr. Beck is not a member.” This was probably Niels R. Beck of Deer Lodge (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Christoffersen, Christian
text: Probably Christen Pedersen (1845–1895), son of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch KWJN-123): the Chris Christofferson whom Shupe lists among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Bertha Hansen, daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, and died at Soda Springs in 1895. A Chris Christofferson, probably he, proved up a 160-acre homestead near Soda Springs (Boise Meridian, T8S R40E, secs. 22–23 and 26), patented August 3, 1888 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-ID0120__.123). The 1880 U.S. census lists “C. Christopherson”, born in Denmark about 1846, and his wife Bertha at Soda Springs (1880 U.S. census).

name: Christoffersen, Peter
text: Peder Christophersen (1810–1891), a Danish convert who came to Utah with his family in 1859 (FamilySearch KWVH-NCY). The Church History Department's pioneer database records that he and his son Andrew signed a Morrisite oath in May 1862. Shupe lists him among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). Father of Mary Christoffersen Anderson; he died at Soda Springs in 1891. A family account in a 1989 county history says the family left Denmark in 1857, that polygamy did not fit their way of life, and that for safety they joined the Morrisites who were going north (Powell County: Where It All Began, p. 111). The Church History Department's pioneer database places them in an 1859 company.

name: Christofferson, Andrus
text: Anders Pedersen (1841–1921), son of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch L2XW-JS2): the Andrew who signed a Morrisite oath with his father in May 1862 (Church History Department pioneer database). Shupe lists Andrew Christoffersen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Christiane Marie Hansen, daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, and died at Deer Lodge, Montana, in 1921. According to the same county history, he tried mining in Idaho, then cattle at Bannack and Virginia City, and in 1874 settled in the Deer Lodge Valley, where he started a dairy (Powell County: Where It All Began, p. 111). His 160-acre homestead in the Deer Lodge Valley (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, sec. 28) was patented on November 23, 1891 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0250__.196). The 1880 U.S. census, however, lists “A. Christopherson”, born in Denmark about 1841, and his wife Katie at Soda Springs, Idaho, so the family may have moved between the two places (1880 U.S. census).

name: Christofferson, Ida
text: Ida Pedersen (1850–1924), daughter of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch L75M-CRD). Shupe lists her among the Morrisite families who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 and says she married Lieutenant Shoemaker, the first soldier married at the fort (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13); Family Tree names her husband as Francis Marion Shoemaker. She died at Sedro-Woolley, Washington, in 1924.

name: Christofferson, Maria
text: Probably Mary Anne Christoffersen (1847–1928), daughter of Peter and Abelone Christoffersen (FamilySearch KWJN-1KY). The first cannon shot at Kington Fort on June 13, 1862, shattered her chin and killed the young mother sitting beside her (Anderson, p. 119); Anderson quotes her as a witness to Morris's death (Anderson, p. 140). Anderson gives her age as seventeen and as fifteen; Family Tree gives her birth as July 20, 1847. She married Niels Anderson at Soda Springs in 1863, on July 30 (Anderson, p. 162) or July 20 (the family gravestone and Shupe, p. 13), and died there in 1928. The roll has two Marias; which entry is hers is not certain. At Robert T. Burton’s trial in February 1879 “Mrs. Mary Anderson” testified for the prosecution that she had lived at Soda Springs sixteen years and had been with the Morrisites in 1862 ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 21, 1879): almost certainly she. The Ogden Junction ’s report of the same testimony has her say that the cannon ball “took off my chin; it killed a lady beside me,” and that she saw “Morris and Banks and Mrs. Swanee and Mrs. Bowman, who were killed” (February 22, 1879, p. 4).

name: Christofferson, Matilda
text: Probably Matthia Pedersen (1840–1908), daughter of Peter Christoffersen (FamilySearch LHFM-68F). She married Lars Hansen, son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, so she is probably the Mrs. Matilda Hansen whom Shupe lists at Soda Springs in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). She died at Grand Forks, British Columbia, in 1908.

name: Lee, Andrew
text: Andrew Lee (1818–1863; FamilySearch 2ZS4-6YS), husband of Charlotte Lee; Family Tree says they joined the Morrisite movement together. At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor; he was also among the men tried for resisting an officer (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a George Lee among the seven instead (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31). Holley says Andrew Lee died before the trial and that his widow Charlotte then married a soldier, Charles Cooney (Holley, UHQ 2008), but the court report shows him alive and sentenced in March 1863; Family Tree gives his death that year.

name: Lee, Charlotte
text: Charlotte Lee (1822–1865; FamilySearch L5F4-44L). Family Tree says she and her husband, Andrew Lee, came to Utah in the James Brown company, joined the Morrisite movement and were excommunicated.

name: Hanson, Christian
text: Probably Christiane Marie Hansen (1846–1927), daughter of Rasmus and Lena Hanson (FamilySearch MG21-P6Q). She married Andrus (Anders) Christoffersen and lived and died in the Morrisite community at Deer Lodge, Montana. The roll has two Christian Hansons.

name: Hanson, Hans
text: Probably Hans Rasmus Hansen (1838–1911), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson (FamilySearch KF11-1MK). Shupe lists Hans Hansen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863, along with a Mrs. Amelia Hansen (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13); Hans Rasmus married Christine Amalia Christoffersen. He died at Blackfoot, Idaho, in 1911. He may instead be the roll's second Rasmus Hanson; which man is which is not settled.

name: Hanson, Lars
text: Probably Lars Hansen (1842–1911), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, who came to Utah with the family in 1859 (FamilySearch LY9T-Z79). Shupe lists a Lars Hansen among the Morrisites who came to Soda Springs with General Connor in May 1863 (Shupe, Caribou County Chronology, p. 13). He married Matilda Christoffersen and died at Grand Forks, British Columbia, in 1911. The roll also has a Lars Christian Hanson. A Lars Hansen, probably he, received patents for land near Soda Springs in section 22, next to Chris Christofferson’s homestead: a 160-acre cash entry patented in 1891 and another tract in 1896 (Boise Meridian, T8S R40E; BLM General Land Office records, accessions STA-ID0020__.206 and STA-ID0090__.326). In 1880 Lars Hansen, born in Denmark about 1841, and his wife Matilda were living at Soda Springs (1880 U.S. census).

name: Cook, Ellen
text: Probably Ellen Haworth (born 1820), wife of Richard Cook (FamilySearch LCCJ-LS7, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Hellen Cook”).

name: Cook, Hannah
text: Probably Hannah Peek (1814–1895), who married Richard Cook in 1854 and died in Nevada (FamilySearch LZW3-1Q2, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Hannah Cook”).

name: Cook, Margaret
text: Margaretta Julia Greatrix (1828–1888), wife of John Cook (FamilySearch LHV7-2NX); she lived at Franktown, Nevada, in 1880 and died at Mottsville in the Carson Valley. She belonged to the Morrisites until 1870 and was baptized into the RLDS Church at Sheridan, Nevada, in September 1873 (Black, Early Members of the Reorganized Church, vol. 2, s.v. “Cook, Margaretta”). A Margaret Cook, probably she, interpreted a tongue given through Morris in a fellowship meeting at Weber on March 9, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 634). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Margaret Cook”).

name: Cook, Sarah
text: Probably Sarah Rostron (1823–1893), wife of John Cook and widow of James Cooper Holt, whose four children are on the roll (FamilySearch KWJ4-74G, probable match). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Sarah Cook”). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (two files, 7 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 12280).

name: Cook, Mary
text: Probably Mary Cook (1841–1904; FamilySearch LCCP-6HT, probable match). Family Tree gives her as a wife of John Cook, but the 1860 census lists her, with two small children, in Richard Cook’s household at Kaysville. Her later children, by William J. White, were born in the Carson Valley from 1863; she died at Palouse, Washington. On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Mary Cook”).

name: Brooks, Nathan
text: Probably Nathan Brooks (1793–1881), who died at South Weber (FamilySearch KWJH-PH6, probable match); his wife Elizabeth (Betty Smith) is also on the roll. On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Nathan Brooks”). One of the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, to found his church, and made a high priest (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives, as “Nathan Brookes”). Aged 67, he was among the men discharged at the fort on June 16, 1862 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library).

name: Kendell, Johanna
text: Joanna Peek (1827–1900), wife of William Kendell Jr. (FamilySearch KWN2-QT3). On February 11, 1861, she was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Joanna Kendall”).

name: Morrison, Niels
text: Named with John Trolsen and Niels Jacobson in a revelation (Spirit Prevails, p. 257). In the winter of 1864 six Morrisite apostles met with Richard Cook in Neils Morrison’s house in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 178, 180). On February 11, 1861, he was among the South Weber followers of Morris cut off from the LDS Church on the motion of the apostle John Taylor, seconded by Wilford Woodruff (Woodruff, journal, February 11, 1861, as “Nels Morrison”).

name: Jones, William J.
text: Very probably the William Jones whose departure from the camp led to the siege. One of Morris’s first converts, he left the fort in the spring of 1862, was captured with John Jensen and Lars Gurtsen by an armed party under Peter Klemgard, and was held in a log house at the fort, chained, until June 13, 1862; the writs issued over his detention brought the posse (Anderson, pp. 97–100, 107). Revelation concerning him: Spirit Prevails, pp. 503–5. Forscutt says that in 1861 he was arrested by Constable Burton and rescued by his brethren, and that he later left the camp (Forscutt, Sketch, MS pp. 39, 44). Eardley names him as the man who went to John Banks’s wagon after the surrender (Gems, p. 28). Family Tree identifies him as William J. Jones (1825–1909), a Welsh convert who emigrated in 1855; a family life sketch there says he joined the Morrisites in April 1861 and escaped from the fort, and later testified for the defense at Burton’s trial. His wife Ann (Anne Haddock) and his mother Margaret are probably the Ann and Margaret Jones listed after him on the roll; Anderson says his wife, mother and three children stayed in the fort when he left. He farmed at South Weber from 1864 and died there in 1909 (FamilySearch K2W1-SRR, probable match).
