name: Geertsen, Lars Christian
text: Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925), born in Denmark, who reached Utah in September 1861 (FamilySearch LHN8-BJ8): the Lars Gurtsen (Lewis C. Gurtsen) who, having left the camp, was captured with William Jones and John Jensen by Peter Klemgard’s party in the spring of 1862 and held with them in a log house at the fort. After several days he and Jensen cut a hole through the log wall; Gurtsen escaped, and Jensen was caught and returned (Anderson, pp. 98–100, 105). The Church History Department’s biographical profile of Lars Christian Geertsen (1832–1925) says that he escaped and went to Salt Lake City to tell the authorities that Jones and Jensen were being held against their will, and that the posse followed. A Montana county marriage record spells his name L. C. Gurtson, and the 1880 U.S. census lists him as Louis C. He and his Danish wife came to the Salmon area of Idaho in 1866 or 1867; he homesteaded a cattle ranch at Geertson Creek in 1868, served for a time as a territorial justice of the peace, and between 1872 and 1883 built a two-story hewn-log house that also held the ranch commissary, which served travelers on the Red Rock–Salmon City stage line, and a dance hall used into the 1920s. The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980. He was one of the original shareholders of the Salmon City Cemetery Association, and he died at his homestead on Geertson Creek, near Salmon, on October 3, 1925; his funeral was held at the Methodist church (Idaho

name: Davies, William
text: William W. Davies (1833–1906), born in Denbighshire, Wales, who came to Utah in 1855 (FamilySearch LRMD-8L5). With his wife Anne Elizabeth, also on the roll, he joined Morris; he was held to bail after the siege as “Wm. Davies” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). He was in Montana with the Morrisites by 1864 (an 1882 county history, drawing on Davies, puts him near Virginia City in 1864 and in the Deer Lodge Valley from 1865 to 1867; Watson, p. 189) and from 1867 led the Morrisite community near Walla Walla, Washington, known as the Kingdom of Heaven, until it broke up after the lawsuit of 1880–81 (Anderson, pp. 157, 187–92). He later lived in San Francisco, where James Dove found him in 1892 (Anderson, p. 192), returned to Walla Walla County shortly before his death on November 25 or 26, 1906, and is buried in the Lyons Cemetery above the old community (FamilySearch; Find a Grave 15969383). In 1880 Asa B. Cilley, Thomas W. Evans and A. J. Courtney sued him, his son Alfred (William Alfred Davies, born 1858) and W. Wood in the territorial district court at Walla Walla to collect wages and debts, the case the state archives index calls the “Walla Walla Jesus” case (Washington State Archives, Frontier Justice, WAL-3153). The 1880 U.S. census, taken that June, lists him at Walla Walla as “William W. Davis”, 47, a mason and a widower, with eight children from Grace, 25, to Seth, 4; Arthur and David are not among them. The census mortality schedule for the year records the deaths of Art

name: Bowman, John
text: Probably John Bowman (1824–1898), born at Kirkcaldy, Fife, who came to Utah in 1853 and married Agnes Patton, the roll’s Agnes Bowman, in 1845; he lived at Kaysville in 1870 and at South Weber in 1880 (FamilySearch KWJN-MJF, probable match). Family Tree gives his death as July 31, 1898, at Ogden; the Daughters of Utah Pioneers index gives August 31, 1897, at South Weber (DUP pioneer histories index, no. 3546). A John Bowman went from Soda Springs to Salt Lake City with George Thompson in 1865 to visit the Prophet Cainan, and later he and his wife were in James Dove’s Morrisite group in Nevada (Anderson, pp. 168, 178). Whether he is the “James Bowman” of the June 1862 prisoner list, whose wife was killed at the surrender, is not settled.

name: Bowman, Agnes
text: Probably Agnes Patton (1825–1890), born in Fife, Scotland, wife of John Bowman; she died at South Weber (FamilySearch LHFY-WFT, probable match; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 3537).

name: Moss, Joseph
text: Probably Joseph Moss (1806–1878) of Leigh, Lancashire, whose family came to Utah with the Edward Martin handcart company in 1856 and lived in Davis County in 1860 (FamilySearch KWJW-H3T, probable match). The Mosses on the roll match his household: his wife Mary (Mary Brabin) and their children Peter (Peter John), Joseph Jr., Edward, James, Hiram R. (Hyrum Ralph) and Alice; Elizabeth is not yet placed. By 1870 the family was in Nevada, and he died at Austin, Nevada, in 1878. In 1878, John R. Eardley wrote, he was returning from Austin to his son Joseph’s house when “a severe snow storm” overtook him; “he was found 2 or 3 days afterwards in a ravine, frozen stiff” (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880). Williams wrote of him as “Moss in Nevada” in August 1873 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873).

name: Moss, Mary
text: Probably Mary Brabin (1810–1883), wife of Joseph Moss, born at Leigh, Lancashire; she died at Austin, Nevada (FamilySearch KWJ4-JBY, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41659).

name: Moss, Edward
text: Probably Edward Moss (1835–1889), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, born at Ashton-under-Lyne (FamilySearch KWJW-H35, probable match). Held to bail after the siege as “Ed. Moss” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Family Tree records his enlistment at Camp Douglas, the post of Connor’s California Volunteers, in February 1863, and his discharge in 1866; he died at Austin, Nevada, in 1889. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41657).

name: Moss, James
text: Probably James Moss (1844–1915), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, born at Ashton-under-Lyne; in Nevada by 1870, he died at Boise, Idaho (FamilySearch KWVP-QWL, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 41655).

name: Chamberlain, James
text: Probably James Chamberlain (1848–1925), born at the Cape of Good Hope, son of Mary Allen Chamberlain, who is also on the roll with two of her daughters; he died at Salt Lake City (FamilySearch KWCY-SXF, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (two files, 9 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 37732).

name: Cowan, James Jr.
text: Probably James Cowan (1833–1895), born at Glasgow, son of James and Janet Cowan, who are also on the roll; he died at Slaterville (FamilySearch KWC4-JQV, probable match). The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of him (3 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 42274). A James Cowan was called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 142; Anderson, p. 67); which of the two James Cowans on the roll is not settled.

name: Park, Ann
text: Probably Ann Brooks Park (1811–1889), born at Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, wife of David Park; the family went to the Carson Valley, Nevada, where she died (FamilySearch KWJ5-6FF, probable match). She was not related to the Brooks family on the roll. The Daughters of Utah Pioneers hold a pioneer history of her (two files, 11 pages; DUP pioneer histories index, no. 22908).

name: Moss, Peter
text: Peter I. Moss, named in the complaint after the November 1861 fight at the schoolhouse (Anderson, p. 82); a revelation of March 22, 1862, concerns his imprisonment (Spirit Prevails, pp. 471–72). Probably Peter John Moss (1837–1883), son of Joseph and Mary Moss, held to bail after the siege as “Peter J. Moss” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); he died in Idaho in 1883 (FamilySearch KWJC-HWG, probable match). Forscutt records his arrest at Farmington in March 1862: he was tried, fined and sentenced to forty days at hard labor, and wrote to his wife, “I shall not flinch from my principles” (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University; the entry is written “Mar 17/63,” but its place in the diary puts it in 1862).

name: Higham, Charles
text: Charles Higham (1823–1891), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Jane in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LV14-G51). Held to bail after the siege as “Chas. Higham” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); Holley names him among the Slaterville and Marriott men taken prisoner (Holley, UHQ 2008). About 1877 George Williams wrote from England that “Bro Higham that was at Weber & now lives out Snake river” had visited George Thompson there and told “of great trouble with Indians” (Williams to William James, Church History Library, MS 31876). He died at Blackfoot, Idaho, in 1891. His wife Jane was George Thompson’s sister (see her note).

name: Higham, Jane
text: Jane Thompson (1824–1894), born in England, wife of Charles Higham, also on the roll; married in 1850, they crossed together in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch K2VD-7R9). She died in Bonneville County, Idaho, in 1894. She was the elder sister of George Thompson (1826–1894), Williams’s companion at Walthamstow and later president of the Montana church: both were christened at Ashwicken, Norfolk, children of Thomas Thompson and Jane Hunter (FamilySearch K2VD-7R9, K2JF-6VH). In 1891 Thompson, widowed, settled at Basalt, Idaho, near his daughter Emma, and wrote that “my sister Mrs. Higham” lived about four miles north (Thompson to Eardley, October 1891, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1891). She is buried at Grove City Cemetery, Blackfoot.

name: Klingbeck, Jacob C.
text: Jacob Carl Frantsen Klingbech (1812–1897), born in Denmark, who came to Utah with his wife Karen Marie and their children in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859, the Danish company that also brought the Hanson, Christoffersen and Sorenson families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch L4SL-HCW). In 1860 the family was at Moroni, Sanpete County, where he was enumerated as Jacob C. Clingbeck, farmer, with Caroline M. and Fredk W. (1860 U.S. census, Sanpete County). He died at Emmett, Idaho, in 1897. The Church History Library holds a Danish journal, circa 1857–1877, of Johan Frederik Fransen Klingbaek (1815–1885), recounting church work in Denmark, emigration to Utah, and his associations with the Morrisites and then the Reorganized Church (MS 8268, on microfilm). How he was related to Jacob Carl Frantsen Klingbech, whose patronymic he shares, is not yet known, and the journal has not yet been read for this guide.

name: Klingbeck, Karen M.
text: Karen Marie Christensen (1824–1898), born in Denmark, wife of Jacob Carl Klingbech since 1843 (FamilySearch L4SL-HXF); in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 with her husband and children (Church History Biographical Database). The 1860 census at Moroni gives her as Caroline M. (1860 U.S. census, Sanpete County).

name: Klingbeck, Frederick V.
text: Frederik Waerenth (Verner) Klingbech (1850–1931), born in Denmark, son of Jacob Carl and Karen Marie Klingbech, with whom he crossed in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch MNJV-Z9R). About eleven in 1861.

name: Nuttor, William
text: William Nutter (1830–1906), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Dinah in the John Smith Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-4FB); the roll spells the name Nuttor. They later settled in Nebraska, where he died at Shelton, Buffalo County, in 1906.

name: Nuttor, Dinah
text: Dinah Ingham (1834–1918), born in England, wife of William Nutter since 1852; they crossed together in the John Smith Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJ4-VQY). She died at Shelton, Nebraska, in 1918.

name: White, William
text: William J. White (1841–1917), born in England, son of William and Rhoda White, who came to Utah with his mother (the roll’s Rhoda Jones) and his sisters Hannah and Sarah (the roll’s Sarah Harris) in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LCCL-MLL). Held to bail after the siege as “William White” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862); Holley names him among the Slaterville and Marriott men taken prisoner (Holley, UHQ 2008). Family Tree gives his marriage in 1862 to Mary Cook, also on the roll; their children were born in the Carson Valley, Nevada, from 1863. He died at Spokane, Washington, in 1917. On November 9, 1875, John R. Eardley wrote from Hollister, California, that “Wm. White has also settled a few miles from here” (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23); whether this was William J. White, whose family is placed in the Carson Valley, is not certain.

name: White, Hannah
text: Hannah White (1844–1868), born in England, daughter of William and Rhoda White and sister of William J. White and Sarah Harris, all on the roll with their mother as Rhoda Jones; she crossed with them in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-43K). She married in 1864 and died at Dayton, Nevada, in the Carson Valley where many Morrisites settled, in 1868.

name: Mather, John O.
text: Called to the apostleship with Richard J. Livingstone, March 25, 1862 (Spirit Prevails, p. 476), and held to bail after the siege as “J. O. Mather” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Probably John Ogilvie Mather (1822–1910), born in Scotland, who came to Utah in the Milo Andrus Company of 1855 with his wife Mary Magee and their children, among them Helen, born in 1851 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJD-2KP, probable match); the roll lists Mary and Ellen Mather with him. He died at Salt Lake City in 1910. A second Mather family, that of James Higginson Mather, came the same year in another company; the roll’s James Mather may belong to it.

name: Mather, Mary
text: Probably Mary Magee (1822–1888), born in Scotland, wife of John Ogilvie Mather since 1845, who crossed with him in the Milo Andrus Company of 1855 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch M1VV-GHK, probable match). Magee is also a surname on the roll; a family tie to William Magee has not been checked. She died at Salt Lake City in 1888.

name: Mather, Ellen
text: Probably Helen Mather (1851–1919), born at Dundee, daughter of John Ogilvie and Mary Mather, both on the roll; Helen and Ellen were used for the same name (FamilySearch KWJD-LSY, probable match). About ten in 1861. She died at Salt Lake City in 1919.

name: Astel, Joseph
text: Brought word to Morris that George Leslie wanted to hear from him; named in Morris’s letter to Leslie, Weber, July 9, 1861 (Spirit Prevails, p. 670). Summoned with the second group before the Farmington court-martial for refusing militia training, and fined $56.80 (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 34). Probably Joseph Astle (1829–1862), born in England, who came to Utah with his wife Esther in the Henry W. Miller Company of 1852 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch K27Y-ZFV, probable match). Family Tree gives his death in 1862, with the place as Montana; neither has been checked.

name: Astel, Esther
text: Probably Esther Bamford (1829–1887), born in England, wife of Joseph Astle since 1850, who crossed with him in the Henry W. Miller Company of 1852 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KDMD-WDN, probable match). She remarried in 1864 and died in Montana, where many Morrisites settled, in 1887.

name: Nash, George
text: Probably George Nash (born 1820 in England), who came to Utah with Maria Mitson in the Daniel Robison Company of 1860, the company that brought Mark Hill Forscutt (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJW-263, probable match). Nothing more about him is known yet.

name: Nash, Maria
text: Probably Maria Mitson (born 1817 in England), wife of George Nash in Family Tree, who crossed with him in the Daniel Robison Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KH9K-H9F, probable match).

name: Hegg, Svend
text: Held to bail after the siege as “S. Hagg” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Probably Sven Olasson Hägg (1832–after 1882), born in Sweden, who came to Utah in the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJF-86P, probable match). Family Tree gives his wife as Anna Lundsten (1833–1862), who may be the roll’s Ann Hegg. The Spirit Prevails names the second woman shot at the surrender on June 15, 1862, after Isabella Bowman, as “Mrs. O’Hagg” (p. 8), and Alexander Dow’s affidavit calls her a Danish woman (Anderson, p. 148); she may have been Anna, but the identification has not been checked. The 1870 U.S. census lists Swen Hagg, 37, farming in Walla Walla County, Washington Territory, with John, 10; as Swen O. Hagg he proved up a homestead of 170.62 acres there, patented July 24, 1890 (BLM General Land Office records, accession SER-WAWWAA 016765). In June 1880 “Swin O. Hagg”, 48, born in Sweden, a laborer and a widower, was living in William W. Davies’s dwelling at Walla Walla, with an Ole Hagg, 72, born in Sweden, two houses away (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c). Testifying for Davies in 1881, Swen O. Hagg said he had known him “ever since the fall of 1861,” had joined his association in 1866, and had come to Walla Walla in the fall of 1867 with the first members, five families of about forty people; in Davies’s teaching he was the central figure of the second of the circles around the Trinity. Ola Hagg, 73, who had come to

name: Babbington, Thomas
text: Probably Thomas Bebbington (1801–1866), born in England, who came to Utah in the Robert L. Campbell Company of 1854, the company of the Kendell and Higham families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch LHDG-13K, probable match). He died at Ogden in 1866.

name: Baxter, Henry
text: Probably Henry Baxter (1806–1865), born in Scotland, who came to Utah with his family in the John A. Hunt Company of 1856 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJJ-G92, probable match). His wife Agnes Grant died in 1860, so the roll’s Agnes Baxter is perhaps another member of the family. A “Mrs. Baxter” was later in James Dove’s Morrisite group (Anderson, p. 178); which Baxter is not known. He died in Cache County in 1865.

name: Loasle, John C.
text: Hans Kasper (John Kasper) Loosli (1831–1901), born at Dürrenroth, Bern, Switzerland, who married Anna Elisabeth Hunsperger, the roll’s Anne Elizabeth Loasle, in 1857 and came to Utah in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWNF-BGT). Held to bail after the siege as “J. G. Lousley” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Family Tree records later marriages in Utah from 1881, one of them in the Endowment House in 1882, which suggests he returned to the Latter-day Saints; he died at Clarkston, Cache County, in 1901.

name: Loasle, Anne Elizabeth
text: Anna Elisabeth Hunsperger (1835–1923), born in Switzerland, wife of Hans Kasper Loosli since 1857, with whom she came to Utah in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860 (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWNF-BGR). She died in Utah in 1923..

name: Trahern, John
text: Probably John W. Treharne (born 1824), who crossed in the James Darling Ross Company of 1860, the company of the Bar and Rodgers families on the roll (Church History Biographical Database), and probably the “John Trehan” held to bail after the siege (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). Not yet found in Family Tree.

name: Jones, William
text: Probably William Jones (born 1803 in England), who married Rhoda White, the roll’s Rhoda Jones, about 1860; Family Tree records him in Weber County in 1860 and his excommunication from the LDS Church at Weber on March 31, 1861 (FamilySearch LWFK-BKP, probable match). He is not the William J. Jones whose capture and detention at the fort in the spring of 1862 brought the posse (see Jones, William J.); which of the two the other references to a William Jones mean has not been settled.

name: Jones, Rhoda
text: Rhoda White (1811–1890), born at Bricketwood, Hertfordshire, widow of William White (died 1842), who came to Utah in the Charles A. Harper Company of 1855 with her children William J., Hannah and Sarah White, all three on the roll, Sarah as Sarah Harris (Church History Biographical Database; FamilySearch KWJQ-PBL). She married William Jones, who precedes her on the roll, about 1860. She went to Nevada with her children and died at Dayton, in the Carson Valley, in 1890.

name: Nielson, Christian
text: Remanded to prison with Peter Klemgaard after the siege, while the other men were held to bail (Deseret News, June 25, 1862). At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to twelve years at hard labor, the second-heaviest sentence; the defence called Robert T. Burton to testify about him (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Pardoned a few days later by Governor Harding (Spirit Prevails, p. 8, and Gems, p. 31, as Christian Nelsen or Nelson).

name: Christiansen, Jens
text: At the March 1863 term he was convicted of murder in the second degree and sentenced to ten years at hard labor, and he was also named among the men tried for resisting an officer (Deseret News, April 1, 1863); pardoned a few days later (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31).

name: Mason, Andrew
text: Probably the Andrew M. Mason convicted of murder in the second degree at the March 1863 term and sentenced to ten years at hard labor (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems do not name him among the seven, listing John E. Jones in his place (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31).

name: Lee, George
text: The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a George Lee among the seven Morrisites sentenced in March 1863 (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31), but the court report names Andrew Lee, also on the roll, and no George Lee (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). A George Lee, 71, born in New York, was living at Walla Walla in June 1880, two houses from William W. Davies, among other former Morrisites (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c); whether he is the roll’s George Lee is not known.

name: Nielson, John
text: Held to bail after the siege as “John Neilson” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) and named among the men tried for resisting an officer in March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). The Spirit Prevails and Gems name a John Nielson among the seven sentenced for murder (Spirit Prevails, p. 8; Gems, p. 31); the court report has a “Kadrup Neilsen” among the seven instead.

name: Hewitt, Philip
text: Testified for the defence at the trial of Peter Klemgard and others, March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Perhaps Phillip Hewitt (1803–1882), who came to Utah in 1855 (Church History Biographical Database); not yet confirmed. A Philip Hewitt testified at Burton’s trial in February 1879 that he lived in Salt Lake City’s Twelfth Ward, had been at the camp in 1862 and was a Morrisite ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 25, 1879).

name: Svenson, Peter
text: Testified for the defence at the trial of Peter Klemgard and others, March 1863 (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). Perhaps the Peter Swenson (born 1836) of the Robert F. Neslen Company of 1859 (Church History Biographical Database); not yet confirmed.

name: Rasmussen, Hans C.
text: Hans Christian Rasmussen (born 1816 in Denmark; FamilySearch L6NP-CJX), husband of Caroline Henriette Holm (the roll’s Caroline H.) and father of Peter Frederik Christian and Georg Thorvald (the roll’s Peter F.C. and George T.). The 1870 U.S. census finds the family at Walla Walla, Washington Territory, as “H C Rassmussen”, 54, with children born in Denmark, Utah (about 1860), Idaho (about 1863) and Montana (about 1866), a path that follows the Morrisite settlements at Soda Springs and Deer Lodge.

name: Rasmussen, Caroline H.
text: Caroline Henriette Holm (born 1824 in Denmark; FamilySearch MVC9-941), wife of Hans Christian Rasmussen. Family Tree records her emigration in 1860. She is the “Lena”, 46, of the 1870 U.S. census at Walla Walla.

name: Rasmussen, Peter F.C.
text: Peter Frederik Christian Rasmussen (born 1846 in Denmark; FamilySearch G4PW-RR7), son of Hans Christian and Caroline Henriette Rasmussen; his given names match the roll’s initials. Nothing later is recorded for him in Family Tree.

name: Rasmussen, George T.
text: Georg Thorvald Rasmussen (1848–1916; born at Copenhagen; FamilySearch G4PW-GL6), son of Hans Christian and Caroline Henriette Rasmussen; “Thorvald” matches the roll’s T. With his parents at Walla Walla in the 1870 U.S. census, age 21; he married Elmira Adalaid Cox in 1874 and died in Washington County, Oregon.

name: Livingstone, R. J.
text: Richard John Livingston (1828–1892; born at Liverpool; FamilySearch L4RB-P1W), husband from 1860 of Isabella Napier (the roll’s Isabella); their son John Napier Livingston was born in 1862. Called to the apostleship with John O. Mather (Revelation No. 248, Weber, March 25, 1862; Spirit Prevails, p. 476). Held to bail after the siege as “R. J. Livingston” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) and fined $100 for resisting an officer as “Richard John Livingston” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). As Richard John Livingston he bought 80 acres in Carson Valley as a cash entry at the Carson City land office, patented August 10, 1865 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T13N R19E, sec. 35; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0010__.195). The 1870 U.S. census lists “R J Livingsten” in Douglas County, Nevada (Carson Valley); he died at Walla Walla in 1892. By 1880 he and Isabella were living at Walla Walla: “R. J. Livingston”, born in England about 1828, and his wife Isabella, born in Scotland (1880 U.S. census). Anderson’s “John Livingstone,” prominent in Nevada and among the scattered congregations (Anderson, pp. 3, 143, 157, 172, 177–80), is probably the same man, since his full name was Richard John. In 1877 the Carson Valley News reported that a preacher calling himself the Prophet Daniel had told “the Morrisites” at Genoa of a child born at Walla Walla who was to be the Savior, and that R. J. Livingstone had sold his property and left for Walla Walla “that he may hereafter live and die near

name: Livingstone, Isabella
text: Isabella Napier (1818–1895; FamilySearch L41L-NPL), wife of Richard John Livingston from 1860, after an earlier marriage in 1850. In 1880 she and her husband were living at Walla Walla (1880 U.S. census). She died in Washington in 1895. The “Mrs. Levengston” who put $900 into William W. Davies’s community near Walla Walla and later got it back, according to testimony in 1881, was probably Isabella (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Hanson, Lars Christian
text: Lars Christian Hansen (1832–1889; born at Dronninglund, Denmark; FamilySearch KC44-FBW), husband of Mattie Maria Iverson (the roll’s Mattie Hanson). The 1870 U.S. census finds him farming in the Deer Lodge Valley as “Lewis C. Hansen”, 38, with Mary 38, Joseph 8 (born in Utah) and two children born in Montana. He died at Deer Lodge in 1889. He received two land patents in the Deer Lodge Valley: one paid with agricultural college scrip in 1873, in the same section as Niels R. Beck’s land (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, sec. 34), and a cash entry for 634.84 acres, nearly a full section (T7N R8W, sec. 6), patented March 5, 1890, after his death (BLM General Land Office records, accessions AGS-0353-237 and STA-MT0140__.418). Why one farmer bought so much land is an open question.

name: Hanson, Mattie
text: Mattie Maria Iverson (1830–1897; FamilySearch LYV6-TPP), wife of Lars Christian Hansen; the “Mary” of the 1870 U.S. census at Deer Lodge. She died in Montana in 1897.

name: Olsen, Ole
text: Probably Ole Olsen (1810–1888; FamilySearch KHLF-L26), who died at Deer Lodge. The 1870 U.S. census lists Ole Olsen, 60, born in Denmark, farming in the Deer Lodge Valley ($300 real estate, $700 personal), with Josephine 8, born in Utah; Family Tree gives him a daughter Josephine Victoria, born 1861. Family Tree also gives him a son Lars Olsen (1837–1908); whether he is the roll’s Lars Olsen is not confirmed. On June 30, 1876, Ole Olsen received a patent for 160 acres in the Deer Lodge Valley, paid for with Virginia agricultural college scrip (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, secs. 26–27; BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-411). A Lars Olsen’s scrip patent, signed the same day, covers adjoining land in section 27. His daughter Josephine married George Johnson on July 1, 1876; Johnson, who led the Montana church from 1921 until 1954, was described about 1902 as, with his family, a member of the Morrisite church. The same sketch says Josephine’s father, Ole Oleson, emigrated from Denmark in 1860 and died in June 1888 in what is now Powell County; it gives her birthplace as Wyoming, where the 1870 census has Utah ( Progressive Men of the State of Montana , Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902], pp. 1092–93). The Montana church’s membership record supports the identification: Josephine Victoria Olsen, born at South Weber, Utah, on December 22, 1861, was baptized at Deer Lodge on June 17, 1876, by Jens Jensen and George Johnson and confirmed by Jens Jensen and Ole O

name: Gudmundson, Christian
text: Christian Nielsen Garff (1848–1927; born at Eskebjerg, Denmark; FamilySearch KWDS-VMD), son of Marie Jacobsdatter (the roll’s Mary Gudmundson) by her first marriage, and so stepson of Gudmund Gudmundson. The 1870 U.S. census lists him as Christian, 22, born in Denmark, in Goodman Goodmanson’s household in Salt Lake County. He died at Logan in 1927.

name: Richardson, Jane
text: Probably Jean or Jane Miller (born 1815 in Scotland; FamilySearch GNP1-NDS), wife of James Richardson (born 1810 at Edinburgh; GMQL-V7P), the first James Richardson on the roll; the second is probably their son James (born 1834; GNP1-ZYN). Family Tree places the family at Alton, Illinois, in 1850 and in Douglas County, Nebraska, in 1860. The 1870 U.S. census finds them in the Deer Lodge Valley: James 62, blacksmith; Jane 59; James 36 and William 32, farmers; Alexander 24 and Cornelius 17, miners, born in Illinois. Alexander may be the roll’s “Aerilous”: the bail list prints “Alexander Richardson” (Deseret News, June 25, 1862) and the court report “Alex. Richardson” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863).

name: Richardson, William
text: Probably William Richardson (born 1838 in Scotland; FamilySearch GNP1-C87), son of James and Jane Richardson; farming in his father’s household in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870 U.S. census, age 32. Family Tree has a possible duplicate, PN4F-6R3 (1839–1913), who died at Boise. A William Richardson received a patent for land in the Deer Lodge Valley paid with agricultural college scrip, signed June 30, 1876 (Montana Principal Meridian, T7N R9W, sec. 21; BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-406), and a James Richardson, the father or the son of that name, another nearby in 1880 (sec. 16; accession AGS-0435-027).

name: Bright, Benjamin
text: Benjamin Bright (1850–1927; born in Pottawattamie County, Iowa; FamilySearch KGKV-MXW), son of John G. Bright and Ann Cook, the roll’s John and Ann Bright. The 1860 U.S. census lists him at 9, born in Iowa, and the 1870 U.S. census at 19, a farm hand, both times in his parents’ household (in 1870 under the Kaysville post office, Davis County). He married Josephine Wright Earl in 1890 and died at South Weber in 1927. (Corrected November 4, 2026: an earlier link pointed to a Benjamin Bright born in England in 1855, who reached Utah only in 1867.)

name: Olsen, Lars
text: Perhaps Lars Olsen (1837–1908), whom Family Tree gives as a son of Ole Olsen (Olsen, Ole); not yet confirmed. A Lars Olsen received two patents for land in the Deer Lodge Valley next to Ole Olsen’s: one paid with agricultural college scrip, signed June 30, 1876, the same day as Ole’s (Montana Principal Meridian, T8N R9W, sec. 27), and a 160-acre cash entry patented in 1884 (sec. 22) (BLM General Land Office records, accessions AGS-0353-427 and STA-MT0090__.275). The 1880 U.S. census lists “Lars Oleson”, born in Denmark about 1838, as head of a household at Cottonwood Creek in the Deer Lodge Valley, where Niels R. Beck and Lars C. Hansen also lived (1880 U.S. census); the age fits Ole Olsen’s son.

name: Hanson, Andrus
text: Probably Andrew Hansen (1844–1926), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson, who died at Deer Lodge, Montana (FamilySearch 2Z8Q-CHW); the roll also has an Andrus Hanson Jr., so which entry is his is not certain. An Anders Hansen received a patent for a 160-acre cash entry in the Deer Lodge Valley on June 20, 1883 (Montana Principal Meridian, T9N R9W, sec. 33; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0090__.152).

name: Hanson, Niels
text: Niels Hansen (1851–1938), son of Rasmus and Lena Hanson; at Deer Lodge, Montana, by 1870, and died there (FamilySearch KFK2-MSL). A Niels Hansen, probably he, received a patent for the northeast quarter of section 32 (Montana Principal Meridian, T9N R9W) in the Deer Lodge Valley on February 29, 1896, next to Anders Hansen’s land in section 33 (BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-MT0260__.484).

name: Garrett, John
text: Probably John Garrett (1815–1899), born in England, who died at Blackfoot, Idaho (FamilySearch K2W8-44D, probable match). The 1870 U.S. census lists Jno. Garrett, 50, born in England, a fur trader, with Martha, 50, at a mining camp in Oneida County, Idaho; the roll and Family Tree name his wife Thurza. The 1880 U.S. census settles it: John Garrett, 65, and his wife Thirza, 75, both born in England, were living at Blackfoot, Oneida County, Idaho (1880 U.S. census, Blackfoot, ED 27, p. 323b), so the 1870 “Martha” was probably an enumerator’s error. Between 1882 and 1892 a John Garrett received four patents for land near Blackfoot (Boise Meridian, T3S R35E), each under a different law: a 158.45-acre cash entry (1882), a 160-acre homestead (1888), 200 acres under the Desert Land Act (1890) and a Timber Culture Act claim (1892) (BLM General Land Office records, accessions STA-ID0010__.017, STA-ID0110__.415, STA-ID0020__.148 and TC-0144-330).

name: Park, David Sr.
text: David Park (1809–1884), born at Cambuslang, Lanarkshire, Scotland, husband of Ann Brooks, also on the roll (FamilySearch LLQF-CF6). He received one of the earliest land patents in Carson Valley, Nevada, where many Morrisites settled: a 160-acre cash entry at the Carson City land office, patented December 10, 1864 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, secs. 1–2; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0010__.049). Family Tree places him in Douglas County, Nevada, in 1870. In June 1880 he was at Walla Walla among the members of William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven: “David Park”, 71, born in Scotland, a laborer, sharing a dwelling with Ole Hagg two houses from Davies (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 263c). He returned to the Carson Valley and died at Mottsville on July 22, 1884 (FamilySearch). A list of donations filed in the 1880 suit against Davies credits David Park with $320 between 1874 and 1878 (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Bull, William F.
text: A William F. Bull received a patent for 160 acres near Genoa in Carson Valley, Nevada, where many Morrisites settled, on May 10, 1866 (Mount Diablo Meridian, T12N R19E, sec. 9; BLM General Land Office records, accession STA-NV0010__.258). He is very probably the roll’s William F. Bull: William Field Bull (1819–1896), husband of Agnes Cowan, also on the roll, died at Mottsville in the Carson Valley (FamilySearch KWJN-719), and the 1880 U.S. census lists “W. F. Bull”, born in England about 1820, in the Carson Valley, Douglas County, with his wife Agnes and children born in Utah (James C., about 1860) and Nevada (1872–1879) (1880 U.S. census).

name: Sorenson, Brooer
text: Probably Bror Sörensson (1807–1902), born in Sweden, who died at Walla Walla, Washington (FamilySearch L56J-MC2, probable match); Family Tree gives him two marriages, the second in 1861, and his daughter Celia is also on the roll. In June 1880 a “Sorenson”, 73, born in Sweden, a laborer, was living at Walla Walla among the members of William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven, with a wife of 45 and children Annie, 18, August, 16, and Isaac, 13, born in Utah, and Lena E., 10, born in Washington Territory (1880 U.S. census, Walla Walla, ED 50, p. 264, dwelling 12). The same suit’s list of donations credits “Brrer Sorensen” with a yoke of cattle in 1867, and a witness recalled that “one Mrs. Sorensen” left the community with cattle and a wagon. Testifying for Davies in 1881, Broer Sorenson, 72, said he had known Davies since 1861 and had come with him from Montana in 1867 with his wife and five children, when the community was only five families; he then lived two and a half miles from the camp. Davies named the Sorenson family among those who came with him (Cilley et al. v. Davies, 1880–81).

name: Williams, Thomas
text: A Thomas Williams testified at Robert T. Burton’s trial in February 1879 that he had lived in Ogden since 1865 and had been at South Weber, “called Morris camp,” part of the time in 1862, and was there when the camp was attacked ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 22, 1879). The name is common, and whether he is the Thomas Williams of the roll is not confirmed.

name: Thompson, Emma
text: Daughter of George Thompson, later president of the Montana church, and his wife Frances; born in 1850, the only one of their six children to survive (Anderson, p. 210). As Emma Thompson Just she wrote to a cousin in England in 1864 describing the journey to Soda Springs in May 1863 and the first year there (quoted in Anderson, p. 161). At Burton’s trial in February 1879 “Mrs. Emma Just” testified for the prosecution that she lived in the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho, and had been with the Morrisites on the Weber in 1862 ( Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 22, 1879). She later lived on the Blackfoot River in eastern Idaho, having moved there from Deer Lodge (Anderson, p. 211). Williams wrote from Walthamstow in February 1875 that “Bro Just has a son who has married Bro George’s daughter” (Williams to Andrew Hendrickson, February 5, 1875, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Montana followers, 1874–1875). By the account her daughter Agnes Just Reid published in 1923 as letters from Emma to her father in London, Emma had been divorced in about 1868, left Montana for an aunt’s home in Idaho, and married Nels Just before a justice of the peace at Malad in November 1870; they settled on the Blackfoot River, and her neighbors there included the Garretts of the roll (see John Garrett). The last letter, of May 1, 1891, expects her father back after “twenty-four years of cruel separation” (Reid, Letters of Long Ago , pp. 9–11, 115–18; a late family account).

name: Thomas, William W.
text: Probably William Watkin Thomas of Gwendale, in the upper Deer Lodge valley, Montana. The New North-West names a W. Watkins Thomas, “who has had extensive experience in that business in Wales,” building the roasters and dryers for a works there in 1875; a W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee of the Gwendale railroad meeting of April 1875; a W W Thomas of Gwendale in 1877; and William Watkin Thomas as an administrator of a neighbor’s estate in July 1879. His own estate was being settled by Howell M. Thomas and Thomas C. Porter in August 1882 ( New North-West , April 16, 1875, p. 2; August 6, 1875, p. 3; July 6, 1877, p. 3; July 4, 1879, p. 4; August 11, 1882, p. 4). A William Watkins Thomas took S½ NW¼ and N½ SW¼ sec. 4, T4N R10W, just north of the Evans and Jessen homesteads, with agricultural college scrip, patented June 1, 1872 (BLM General Land Office records, accession AGS-0353-021). This fits Black’s W. W. Thomas, a Welshman baptized into the RLDS Church in 1865 who died in the upper Deer Lodge Valley in 1879. Gwendale was renamed Morristown in 1878, the paper noting that many of its people were Morrisites. No source yet ties him by name to the 1861–62 roll.

name: Thomas, W. P.
text: Probably William P. Thomas of the upper Deer Lodge valley, Montana: a Gwendale election judge in March 1876 with Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen, and in March 1880 one of the Warm Springs settlers (with Daniel James, Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen) whose homestead claims, held up while the land office decided whether the ground was mineral land, were set for hearing; his lay in sec. 34, T5N R10W, on Warm Springs Creek east of where Anaconda was built ( New North-West , March 10, 1876, p. 3; April 30, 1880, p. 4). The claim was patented to him as a homestead on December 10, 1880: N½ SE¼ sec. 33 and N½ SW¼ sec. 34, T5N R10W, 160 acres; he had taken the NE¼ of sec. 33 with agricultural college scrip, patented May 2, 1871 (BLM General Land Office records, accessions STA-MT0220__.277 and AGS-0325-010). Morris names a William Price Thomas, a Welshman, among the first Morrisites in the valley, settling on Warm Springs Creek in 1863 (Morris, Anaconda, Montana , p. 15), and Anderson names W. P. Thomas as William James’s first counselor (pp. 199–200). The Montana church’s membership record, begun when the church was divided into two stakes in July 1874, lists William P. Thomas and Margaretta P. Thomas, both born in Wales and baptized at South Weber, Utah, with William M. James and Daniel James, also Welsh (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folder 7, p. 1). In 1869–70 he was in Britain with George Williams and George Thompson: Thomps

name: Morris, Mary
text: Probably Mary Olsen, a Danish convert and the wife of Joseph Morris; the movement’s own history says he married “Mary Olsen, a Dane,” in August 1861 (Spirit Prevails, “History of Events,” p. 5). After a revelation of August 23, 1861, told Morris to look for “a faithful companion,” he married her shortly afterward; a revelation less than a month after the wedding addressed discord between them, and she remained with him (Anderson, p. 87; Spirit Prevails, pp. 149–51). Their infant son died soon after birth in May 1862 (Anderson, pp. 104–5). Morris’s earlier wives (Mary Thorpe; Elizabeth Mills, 1855; Elizabeth Jones, Provo, 1857) had all left or been separated from him before South Weber (Anderson, pp. 35, 41). His brother George confirms them: Joseph married Mary Thorp in England, and she left him within two months of their reaching Utah in 1853; he then married a widow, Elizabeth Mills, and at Provo “Elize Jones,” from whom church leaders separated him. In 1876 George had “Joseph Morris Jr and Mary his wife” sealed by proxy without saying which Mary (George Morris reminiscences, MS 1614, pp. 115, 117–19, 187). Anderson does not mention the roll’s Karen Morris.

name: Olsen, Anne
text: Probably the wife of Ole Olsen (Olsen, Ole), whose name follows hers on the roll, with Lars Olsen after him. Family Tree gives Ole Olsen a wife Ane Jensdatter, born March 29, 1817, at Adserboe, Melby, Frederiksborg, Denmark, the mother of his children, among them Lars (1837–1908) and Josephine Victoria (1861–1907) (FamilySearch KHWN-B4R). Family Tree gives her death only as before 1870, in the United States, with no source. A sketch of Josephine’s husband, George Johnson, written about 1902, says her mother Anna died in Wyoming in 1862 ( Progressive Men of the State of Montana , Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902], pp. 1092–93). Family Tree also lists, without sources, the family’s emigration in 1859 on the William Tapscott and a residence in Salt Lake County in 1860. An earlier version of this note (November 10, 2026) gave Family Tree’s date for her death as 1870.

name: Lorensen, John Peter
text: Probably Johan Peter Lorentzen, born May 23, 1817, in Holmens parish, Copenhagen (FamilySearch KLVC-XHL), father of the roll’s Charles and Josephine E. Lorentzen. Family Tree does not give a date of death; it says only that he died before 1870, probably in Nevada. Before November 10, 2026, this guide gave his death as 1870 in Nevada, reading that estimate as a date. In the 1870 census his children Charles and Josephine were living at Treasure City, White Pine County, Nevada, in the household of Caroline Laurenson, 52, born in Denmark, with no husband listed (1870 U.S. census, White Pine Co., NV, dwelling 658).

name: Anderson, Christian
text: Probably the Christen Anderson whom the Montana church’s membership record, begun in July 1874, lists as born on Fyn, Denmark, on August 1, 1809, baptized at South Weber, Utah, on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelson, and confirmed by J[oseph] Morris (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folder 7, p. 4). The name is common, and the match rests on the South Weber baptism in 1861, the year the roll was begun.

name: Rasmusson, Rasmus
text: Probably the Rasmus Rasmussen whom the Montana church’s membership record, begun in July 1874, lists as born at Skallerup, Denmark, on October 28, 1830, and baptized at South Weber, Utah, on June 27, 1861; he baptized several of the Omaha and Council Bluffs converts in 1869 and 1870 (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folder 7, pp. 2–5). On February 7, 1869, at Council Bluffs, he was made the church’s first bishop and “first President of the Aaronic order,” an office Williams had given him “according to his birthright” (Omaha minutebook, 1869–1871, MS 31876); in 1869 he was at Omaha City, and Williams called him “the presiding Bishop” there, to whom the accounts of a free-will offering fund were to be rendered (Williams to the Saints at Omaha and Council Bluffs, 1869, MS 31876). As bishop at Race Track he sat on the Montana council from 1881. He refused to sustain William James as president in 1883, kept the church’s books and its reserve-fund deposits, held that Williams’s last letters were not binding because Williams had grown feeble, and said he would wait for the Lord to raise another prophet; the council suspended him as bishop on May 27, 1883 (folder 3, pp. 1–16). The Willow Glen photographs of 1915 captioned “Morrisites” show a Rasmus Rasmussen family; whether it is his is not yet established. name: James, William
text: Probably William M. James (William Morgan James, 1817–1903, in the Church History Library’s catalog), born in Wales and baptized at South Weber, Utah, the first name in the Montana church’s membership record begun in July 1874. He presided over the Warm Spring Creek stake and the Montana council; in 1890 he said Williams and John R. Eardley had sent him from Nevada to preside over the Saints in Montana. Sustained as president of the church in Montana on April 25, 1883, by 19 votes to 10, he claimed the office for life, stayed away from the assembly of April 25, 1886, and was suspended on May 10, 1886, for “usurpation of authority, and heresy”; a meeting in May 1890 failed to reconcile him (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library, folders 7 and 3). In 1873 he was away on “his Mission in Nevada,” and he took back the presidency in Montana on July 20 that year. On February 24, 1878, he presided at the joint council at Race Track that chose Andrew Hendrikson’s land for the Lord’s House, though he had favoured Warm Spring (council minutes, 1873–74 and 1878, MS 31876). He “surrendered during the engagement” of June 13–15, 1862, and was discharged at the fort on June 16 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library; identification with the later Montana leader probable, not checked). Appointed president at the organizing meeting of September 22, 1872, by Willi

name: Merrick, John
text: Possibly the John Merrick whom John R. Eardley, writing from Hollister, California, on November 9, 1875, described as living north of San Francisco, well off, “dealing in fine stock and race horses” (Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1864–1901, MS 31876, Church History Library, folder 23). Eardley names him among old acquaintances from the Morrisite years, but the letter gives nothing more to tie him to the roll. On September 13, 1871, George Williams wrote from England that “Bro Merrick” had set out for Montana “with his cattle,” and that Merrick had “passed thro the order of Birthright and at that time was set apart to preach in his native State”; in 1872 Williams said he had asked Merrick to aid “the European mission,” without reply (Williams to Andrew Hendrikson, MS 31876). The cattle dealer of 1875 is very probably the same man. Before he set out, on August 2, 1871, Williams had warned that the road ran through “a country of Indians” and counseled a good guard (translation from the Danish generated by Claude), and wrote that “he is accepted in the position he left me at Cottonwood”; in November 1871 he had no news yet of “Bro Merrick and Knudson” on the way (Williams to Hendrikson, August 2 and November 1871, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1871 and 1872–1873). Williams wrote in 1872 that Merrick's plan to visit Montana in March was “extraordinary for impudence,” though “when this man visited me at Cottonwood he had

name: Bryne, Moses
text: Probably the “Moses Burnes” whom Josiah D. Price names among the six baptized by Morris on April 6, 1861, to found his church; Price notes that he alone of the six was not made a high priest (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Price, Josiah
text: Josiah D. Price, born April 8, 1832, in Glamorgan, South Wales, by his own record. He was baptized on December 3, 1861, by William Davies and Edward Lloyd, confirmed by Richard Cook and ordained by Morris, and counted himself the “431st person” in the church; he recorded the consecration of property on December 30, 1861, and the oath of February 12, 1862, sworn twelve at a time, and translated Morris’s ordinances and oath into Welsh. Called for trial at the March 1863 term as “Josiah D. Price” (Deseret News, April 1, 1863). His pocket journal, in English and Welsh, copies Morris’s ordinances and the inscription of his scepter, names the six whom Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, and describes the drill and the four horsemen of May 1, 1862, the companies and soldier’s oath of May 26, which he swore, and the Foreshadowing procession of May 30; it also holds a drawing of Morris’s worlds. On September 30, 1862, he sold a yoke of cattle to John E. Jones and hired himself to Jones from October 6 at fifty dollars a month. He was baptized into the Reorganized Church on February 3, 1867, by Robert Murdock, in Oneida County, Idaho Territory (Josiah D. Price journal, 1858–1873, photocopy, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Lundgreen, Christian
text: Probably the Christian Lundgren whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born in Sjælland, Denmark, baptized at South Weber on June 30, 1861, and confirmed by Joseph Morris; an Aaronic priest, he was excluded from the Omaha congregation in 1870 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). On April 28, 1862, Mark H. Forscutt recorded at Kington Fort: “Christian Lundgreen whipped in the fort by 7 women. He had turned traitor, and also helped Mortensen’s wife away in the night time.” He names the women as Maryann Taylor, Amelia Rothwell, Isabella Bowman, Mrs. Sorenson and Mrs. Thomas (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Forscutt’s Sketch tells the story without naming him.

name: Petersen, Hans
text: Probably the Hans Petersen whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber; his name is struck through, and he was excluded in 1870 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Peterson, Kershon
text: Probably Kjersten Petersen, whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Evetofte [?], Sjælland, Denmark, on December 6, 1821, and baptized at South Weber; she was a member of the Omaha congregation from 1869 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Larsen, Niel
text: Probably the Niels Larsen, born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Maren Larsen (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Larsen, Maren
text: Probably the Maren Larsen, born in Sjælland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Niels Larsen (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Christiansen, Mikkel C.
text: Probably the Mikkel Christensen, born in Jutland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Elisa Christensen; both names are struck through, and both were excluded on November 20, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Christiansen, Lese
text: Possibly the Elisa Christensen, born in Jutland, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber, whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists with Mikkel Christensen; she was excluded on November 20, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). The identification rests on the names alone.

name: Guhl, Maren
text: The Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists a “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” born at Horsens, Jutland, and baptized at South Weber; by 1869 she was the wife of Carleton Fellows, and both were excluded on February 5, 1871 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Whether she is this entry or the roll’s Marian Guhl is not known.

name: Guhl, Marian
text: The Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists a “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” born at Horsens, Jutland, and baptized at South Weber; whether she is this entry or the roll’s Maren Guhl is not known (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Bowen, John
text: Possibly the John D. Bowen of Austin, Lander County, Nevada, to whom a revelation of August 20, 1872, sent William James “to assist him in wisely arrangement in his affairs,” calling him “my son J. D. Bowen,” who “has been worthy and felt after my work.” Bowen wrote in Welsh to William P. Thomas from Austin in 1872–74; in October 1874 he wrote that he had lost all his property, but that Cainan was a true prophet who had sent his servant two years before to try to save it (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas, 1871–1874; translation from the Welsh generated by Claude). In 1878, John R. Eardley reported, John Bowen was “extremely bitter” against William James, charging him with “swindling him & reducing him to a state of beggary, he having placed everything into his hands by virtue of the revelation given to Wm James, sending him to Nevada on his mission”; Eardley, who said he knew nothing of it, defended James (John R. Eardley to Williams, Hollister, California, [May] 1878, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to John R. Eardley, 1871–1880). In September 1871 Williams wrote that he was glad Bowen meant to visit Montana; he “may have listened to Josephism,” but should be invited to settle at Deer Lodge “and to compose some suitable Hymns,” and thanked for “sending to my Family” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to William James and Montana followers, 1870–1873). The identification with the roll’s John

name: Warner, Joseph
text: The Joseph Warner, born in Germany, aged 45, who was among the men discharged at the fort on June 16, 1862 (“Morrisite prisoners, 1862 June,” Historian’s Office collected historical documents, CR 100 397, Church History Library). At Burton’s trial in February 1879 he testified that he was born in Germany, came in 1856, and had lived at Providence, where “I had a vision; Joseph Smith appeared to me; for which I was cut off of the Mormon church”; that “I joined Joseph Morris in May, 1861, at Weber”; and that he was in the camp at the siege and saw Morris and Mrs. Bowman shot. He read the court a sermon “half in German and half in broken English” and recited a revelation in full ( Ogden Junction , February 22, 1879, p. 4). Family Tree gives a Joseph Warner born in Hanover in 1816, living in Cache County in 1860, whose wife Ingry (Ingrid), born in Sweden in 1811, is probably the roll’s Ingray Werner (FamilySearch Family Tree, GK43-2XF and GK43-KYD). In 1880 Joseph Warner, sixty-two, born in Germany, widowed, a laborer, was living at South Weber (1880 U.S. census, South Weber, Davis County, Utah, ED 16). He died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September and before October 2, “an indigent person” who “left no relatives”; P. P. Prophet “and others” buried him at county expense and sold his effects, but “the manuscript he had not disposed of,” and was told on October 30 to dispose of it “if he can” (Davis County Court minutes, October 2 and 30, 1893, pp. 462, 470, FamilySearch fi

name: Werner, Ingray
text: Possibly Ingry (Ingrid) Warner, wife of Joseph Warner, whom Family Tree gives as born in Sweden in 1811 and as dying on June 13, 1862, the day the posse’s first cannon shot killed two women at Kington Fort; the death date has no source there and has not been checked (FamilySearch Family Tree, GK43-KYD). See the open question “Who died at Kington Fort?”

name: Thompson, George
text: Probably George Thompson (1826–1894), later president of the Montana church, who gave his birth date as April 16, 1826, in a letter of 1880 (FamilySearch K2JF-6VH, probable match). He had lived in Idaho, and went from Soda Springs to Salt Lake City in 1865 to visit the Prophet Cainan (Anderson, p. 168). In 1869 he was a shoemaker at Ashwicken, near King’s Lynn, Norfolk, where Williams was preaching, and that December at Brighton; from June 1874 he kept a shop in Shernhall Street, Walthamstow, Essex, where Williams lived with him from January 1875 and where he did Williams’s writing in his last illness. In 1880 he planned to sell his business to take Williams to America. By August 1883 he had moved to Thornwood Common, near Epping, and wrote that “I say but little about gospels now … No one here believes as I do so I am very quiet” (Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1883, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from George Thompson to William P. Thomas, 1869–1874). He was elected president of the church in 1886. In his daughter Emma’s letters as published in 1923, he writes in 1891 that his business is sold and he is coming to her in Idaho (Reid, Letters of Long Ago , pp. 115–16; a late family account).

name: Lloyd, Edward
text: With William Davies he baptized Josiah D. Price on December 3, 1861 (Josiah D. Price journal, P26-22 f1, Community of Christ Library Archives).

name: Sorenson, Anders
text: Probably Anders Søndermark (Anders Sørensen in the draft), whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Vrensted, Jutland, Denmark, on January 9, 1821, and baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, by Morris and Mikkelsen; an Aaronic priest, he was excluded with his wife Karen Maria on November 30, 1871 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Sorenson, Kar M.
text: Probably Karen Maria Sørensen Søndermark, whom the Omaha congregation’s register of 1869–72 lists as born at Vrensted, Jutland, Denmark, on October 9, 1822, and baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, with her husband Anders; both were excluded on November 30, 1871 (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Kundson, Hans
text: Probably the Hans Knudsen whom the Council Bluffs register of 1869–71 lists as born on Fyn, Denmark, and baptized at South Weber on July 18, 1861, by Jens Mikkelsen; at Omaha in 1869 he baptized converts with Rasmus Rasmussen and S. P. Guhl (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Council Bluffs), Church of the Firstborn (Morrisites) records, 1869–1890, MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude).

name: Richards, William
text: Probably the Welsh member at Box Elder whom masked men took from a neighbor’s house one night in the winter of 1861–62; he was spared on his oath never to return to Box Elder. Hearing that he had been killed, W. P. and W. W. Thomas fled to the camp at Weber, where Forscutt wrote down their account (Mark H. Forscutt, diary, 1860–62, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University).

name: Mather, James
text: Called to the apostleship in September 1861 (Anderson, p. 67). In August 1873 Mark H. Forscutt called at Galesburg, Illinois, on “Mr James Mather with whom I was acquainted in Utah, South Weber. He is comfortably situated, but has no religious tendencies remaining” (Forscutt, journal, Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University). Whether the Galesburg man is the roll’s James Mather is not settled; Family Tree’s James Mather (KWJJ-BBK) died in Iowa in 1898.

name: Laird, James
text: Summoned with Morris, the Cooks and Parson before the Farmington court-martial in 1861 for refusing militia training (Forscutt, Sketch, MS p. 28). Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households lists a James Laird, born in New York in 1832, son of John Laird, married to Cathrine Smith, daughter of Daniel Smith, and calls him “a polygamist and Morrisite”; his plural wife Mary Bright refused to go with him when he left South Weber after the war (Allred, South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952, 2004, no. 159 and Attachment 3). Catherine and Mary Laird follow him on the roll.

name: Laird, Mary
text: Probably Mary Bright (born 1843 in England), daughter of John Bright and Sarah Webb, and a plural wife of James Laird. South Weber tradition, as compiled by Norma Allred, says she lived in a log cabin near the mountains from about 1858 to 1862, refused to go with Laird when he left South Weber after the war, and married Thomas Henry Peek in 1864 (Allred, South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952, 2004, nos. 5 and 159). Not checked against Family Tree.

name: Morris, Joseph
text: The prophet himself. The printed roll lists his followers, not Morris. His wife Mary Olsen, a Danish convert he married soon after a revelation of August 23, 1861, is probably the roll’s “Mary Morris.” The roll’s “Karen Morris” is not identified. In 1878 James Bowman, at Soda Springs, mentions a debt of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law,” apparently living nearby; he is not named (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). His elder brother George’s reminiscences give his life before Utah, his arrival in the fall of 1853 and his earlier marriages, to Mary Thorp, Elizabeth Mills and “Elize Jones” (see Documents). (Anderson, Revisited , 87, 104–5; The Spirit Prevails , 149–51; George Morris reminiscences, CHL MS 1614, 115–22)

name: Aggerson, Hans
text: Fined $100 for resisting an officer at the March 1863 term; probably the “H. Okensen” held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Edwards, John C.
text: Held to bail as “J. C. Edwards” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Halse, Samuel
text: Held to bail as “Saml. Hulse” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Moffat, Peter
text: Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Neilsen, Kadrup
text: Convicted of murder in the second degree in March 1863 and sentenced to ten years at hard labor; pardoned by Governor Harding. (Deseret News , April 1, 1863)

name: Parr, L.
text: Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862)

name: Peterson, James
text: Fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , April 1, 1863)

name: Rasmussen, Soren Peter
text: Held to bail as “S. P. Rasmusson” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Reese, John E.
text: Held to bail as “J. E. Reese” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Sorenson, John Peter
text: Held to bail as “J. P. Sorensen” in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863)

name: Williamsen, S.
text: Held to bail in June 1862. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862)

name: Williams, George
text: The “Prophet Cainan,” who claimed to be Morris’s successor and led the church that regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s; in January 1879 he wrote that the Montana Saints lived on “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming (see the Chronology). (Anderson, Revisited ; Watson)

name: Hendrikson, Andrew
text: A Danish immigrant who was never a Latter-day Saint, born at Ondrup, Jutland, on July 29, 1843, and baptized into the Morrisite church in the Missouri River at Omaha on January 22, 1869 (“Record of members, circa 1869–1871,” Council Bluffs, MS 32226; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). In October 1869 Williams named him “the Keeper of the Book” for the Omaha and Council Bluffs fund of free-will offerings (Williams to the Omaha church, October 13, 1869, Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters from Cainan to Andrew Henrikson, 1869). Counselor to William James from May 1882; presided over the Montana church from 1886 until his death. His records, kept by his family, are a main source for Anderson’s book. (Anderson, Revisited)

name: Johnson, George
text: Hendrikson’s associate of more than fifty years, likewise never a Latter-day Saint; presided at the Lord’s House near Racetrack from 1921 until shortly before his death at ninety-eight, the last official leader of the Montana church. A county biography of about 1902 says he came to Montana in the summer of 1873, worked in Deer Lodge hotels, and then took up a stock ranch eight miles south of the town, and that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” On July 1, 1876, he married Josephine V. Oleson, a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. (Anderson, Revisited ; Progressive Men of the State of Montana (Chicago: A. W. Bowen, [c. 1902]), pp. 1092–93)

name: Beck, Lars P.
text: Lars Peter Beck. Born in Jylland (Jutland), Denmark; came to America in 1864 and married Maria Christensen at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, on March 7, 1869. Baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Andrew Henriksen and Niels Jensen, with his wife Maria; their eldest daughter had been born at Fremont in 1870. Ordained a Seventy in Montana on November 10, 1872, and a member of the council of the Danish-speaking stake from 1873 to 1883; the council met in his house near Deer Lodge on February 21, 1875, and their daughter Margaret was born at Deer Lodge that May. With his brother Nels J. Beck he met William P. Thomas at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1880. In February 1883 he said he could not see that choosing a president would do the church any good, and he was among the minority who would not accept William James’s election that April; his brother Nels voted for James. On May 26, 1883, the Race Track council released him as a teacher and, with his wife, from membership, saying that the dissenters “had separated themselves from us” (minutes, MS 31876, Minutes, 1883–1884; translation from the Danish generated by Claude). Their children included Annie, Mary Ann, Margaret, Laura, Carl R., Harry H. and Joseph. He died at Deer Lodge on February 21, 1925, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery there. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), and minutebooks, 1872–1874, p. 3, and 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; council minutes, 1873–1883, MS 31876, Church History Library (translations from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303646; FamilySearch Family Tree, LK44-Y7K; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Beck, Maria
text: Born in Slesvig (Schleswig), on January 7, 1847. Married Lars P. Beck (above) at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, in 1869, and was baptized with him at Fremont, Nebraska, on August 20, 1871, by Niels Jensen and Andrew Henriksen; the family settled near Deer Lodge, Montana, by 1875. Her maiden name was Christensen (Christiansen on her Find a Grave memorial). She died on May 13, 1938, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library (translation from the Danish generated by Claude); Find a Grave 67303647; FamilySearch Family Tree, L4QB-7GT; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Beck, Nels J.
text: Nels Jensen Beck, brother of Lars P. Beck (above). Born at Jernved, near Ribe, Denmark, on May 6, 1847; came to America in 1872 and married Marie Helen Hansen at Deer Lodge that year; lived on Cottonwood Creek. The Montana council minutes of May 29, 1880, name “Lars Beck” and “his brother Niels Beck.” At the general assembly of April 25, 1883, “Nels Beck” and his wife voted to sustain William James, while Lars voted against. On April 25, 1887, “N. J. Beck” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House, with George Johnson and Emmanuel Strome, so that the building would not be taxed. Other “Niels Beck” entries in the minutes may be he or the roll’s Niels R. Beck. He died on October 4, 1921, and is buried at Hillcrest Cemetery, Deer Lodge. (Council minutes, May 29, 1880, MS 31876, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; minutebook, 1881–1890, pp. 10–11, MS 32226, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, GB7W-C7D; family tree compiled by descendants of Lars and Maria Beck, shared by the Richardson family (2026))

name: Strom, Emanuel
text: In a note in his record book he gives his birth year as 1846 and says he was received into “the church of the Saints of the Most High God” at Omaha, Nebraska, in 1872 (day and month uncertain; translation from the Swedish generated by Claude). That year he copied Williams’s epistles and Morris’s revelations into Swedish. In March 1887, when Eardley went east, “Brother Strom” was to conduct the meetings, and on April 25, 1887, “Emmanuel Strome” was made one of the three trustees of the Lord’s House. In 1924 he wrote, and signed “E Strom,” that a feeling had explained to him “the League of Nation, to be united and ready when the Lord want them,” and that a voice had said “1926 Salt Lake City shall be destroid and laid waist.” He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In January 1880, after a visiting preacher named Brand had spoken in the Lord’s House, he said that no “sectarian” preacher should speak there; in May he put to the council a question about Adam and Eve and the serpent, and was asked to bring his violin to the Fourth of July at Deer Lodge. In May 1881 he would not take the sacrament from Erik Eliason, who he said “had come forward and set himself in Cainan’s place and would not take counsel” (translations from the Danish generated by Claude). On February 20, 1880, at Lower Warm Spring Creek, he married Mary Josephine Hellstrom, daughter of Johan Helström (below). He died on January 2, 1929, and is buried at Anaconda. (Record of epistles from Cainan, 1868–1872, and Record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; council minutes, 1876, 1880 and 1881, MS 31876, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrickson, March 11 and 18, 1887, and elections and court, 1886–87, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, K4YW-8YS)

name: Helström, Johan
text: Very probably the “Johan Helström,” born May 1, 1834, in “Dalene” [Dalarna?], Sweden, whom the Omaha register lists as baptized at Fremont, Nebraska, on March 25, 1871, with Maria Helström. Family Tree has Johan Hellstrom born on April 29, 1834, at Gagnef, Dalarna; emigrated in 1864; died at Anaconda, Montana, on March 31, 1913. His daughter Mary Josephine married Emanuel Strom (above) in 1880. His son Peter Helstrom’s wife and children were to be baptized at Race Track on August 9, 1893. He sat on the Race Track council in 1876 and 1880. In 1876 the council heard a letter from Strom about his drinking, and in January 1880 it forgave him, after he had admitted being “under drink” and making threats over land, on condition that he give up strong drink “except the use of the wine at the Lord’s Supper” (translation from the Danish generated by Claude). (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), nos. 31–32, MS 32226, Church History Library; Eardley to Hendrickson, July 27, 1893, and council minutes, 1876 and 1880, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KFR2-9KR)

name: Nielsen, Peter
text: Born at Aalborg, Jutland, Denmark, on February 27, 1833. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on June 26, 1870, by Rasmus Rasmussen and Andrew Hendrikson. He went to Montana, and on July 27, 1887, Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Deer Lodge, as “Peter Neilson,” with members of his family; the branch register marks him as since deceased. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 27 and no. 25)

name: Thorkelsen, Niels
text: Born at Lyby [?], Skåne, Sweden, on March 3, 1823. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on July 22, 1871, by Andrew Hendrikson and Jens Jensen, with Pernelle Tyrkelsen; the draft register notes that he moved to Montana. In October 1890 he was baptized into the Reorganized Church in the Deer Lodge Valley, entered as “Neil Tarkelson.” Family Tree has Niels Torgelson, born March 4, 1823, at Lyby, Malmöhus, Sweden, husband of Pernilla Bengtsson (1824–1891), who died at Anaconda, Montana, on June 9, 1913. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 37 and no. 61; FamilySearch Family Tree, K2HT-982)

name: Jensen, Niels
text: Born in Jutland, Denmark, on March 12, 1829. Baptized into the Morrisite congregation at Omaha on March 12, 1869, by Jens Jensen, and confirmed by S. P. Guhl; in 1869 he led the district at Florence under the Omaha congregation, and at Fremont in 1871 he baptized new members with Hendrikson. He kept a record book of Williams’s letters in Danish copies, 1870–79, which also holds a letter of 1875 from the claimant Barnet Moses Giles (see Repositories ). About March 1890 Joseph C. Clapp baptized him into the Reorganized Church at Willow Glen, Montana, with a Mary Jensen, born January 16, 1828, very probably his wife Maren, whom the Omaha register gives as born June 16, 1828. Family Tree has Niels Jensen, born March 12, 1829, at Smidstrup, Vejle, Denmark, married in 1851 to Maren Sørensdatter (1828–1914); he died at Deer Lodge, Montana, on November 22, 1914. The identification of the Montana Niels Jensen with the Omaha one rests on the matching birth date and wife. See How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? (“Record of members, 1869–1872” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; Record of the Deer Lodge Branch, Montana District (#228), Community of Christ Library Archives, no. 16 and nos. 59–60; Niels Jensen record, 1870–1879, MS 31876, Church History Library; FamilySearch Family Tree, KH45-1ZT)

name: Andrews

name: Cilley, Asa B.

name: Bowman, Isabella
text: Killed at Kington Fort during the surrender, one of the two women shot by Robert T. Burton’s party. Burton was indicted for her killing in 1870 (the indictment was voided in 1872) and again in 1877, tried from February 18, 1879, and acquitted. Alexander Dow’s affidavit of April 1863 calls her “Mrs. Bowman, wife of James Bowman.” The 1891 Salt Lake Tribune letter says she was holding Joseph March’s baby, whom she had taken in after its mother was killed. Wife of James Bowman (below), who was still a believer at Soda Springs in 1878. Not on the printed roll; she may have joined after it was made. South Weber City’s cemetery records say that “Bella Bowman” was buried outside the Pioneer Cemetery fence near its northeast corner. (Salt Lake Herald and Salt Lake Weekly Tribune , Feb.–Mar. 1879 (Burton trial); Salt Lake Tribune , July 26, 1891; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman); Anderson, Revisited , 148–49; South Weber City cemetery records)

name: Bowman, James
text: Husband of Isabella Bowman, who was killed at the surrender. Held to bail in June 1862; fined $100 for resisting an officer in March 1863; moved to Idaho in the spring of 1863. In 1879 he testified at Burton’s trial that he had lived at Soda Springs since 1863. In August 1878 he wrote from Soda Springs to Erick Eliason in Montana, signing himself “yours truly in the New Covenant”; he had received “the Epistle so kindly sent me by the friends in Deer Lodge” and passed it on to “Father Christofferson,” and among debts owed him he lists one of “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” (Church History Library, MS 31876, Letters to Andrew Hendrickson, 1872–1878). Not the John Bowman of the roll, who was at Kaysville in 1870 and South Weber in 1880; Anderson also treats them as two men. Norma Allred’s compilation of South Weber households lists “James & Sarah A.” Bowman in a log house there in 1860 and says that Sarah died in the cannon attack of June 13, 1862 (Norma Earl Allred, comp., South Weber Homes and Families, 1852–1952 (2004), no. 44); the name and the manner of death differ from the contemporary accounts of Isabella Bowman, and the compilation gives no source for them. (Deseret News , June 25, 1862, and April 1, 1863; Salt Lake Herald , Feb. 21, 1879; Anderson, Revisited , 148, 162; Church History Biographical Database (Isabella Bowman))

name: Søndermark, Anders

Søndermark” of the Fremont council of November 30, 1871, who said he believed “J. Morris was a Prophet.” Excluded from the Omaha congregation on November 30, 1871. Not on the printed roll. (“Record of members, 1869–1872,” and its draft, “Record of members, circa 1869–1871” (Omaha), MS 32226, Church History Library; translation from the Danish generated by Claude; Fremont council minutes, November 30, 1871, MS 31876)
